Most of this is native, behind **fullscreen rendering** (`/tui fullscreen`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1`):

([fullscreen](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/fullscreen.md#search-and-review-the-conversation))
- In the classic renderer the transcript view has no search or scroll keys.
- **Scroll keybindings** are rebindable in fullscreen (`Scroll` context: `scroll:top`, `scroll:pageUp`, ...), and the mouse wheel works (`CLAUDE_CODE_SCROLL_SPEED`). ([keybindings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/keybindings.md#scroll-actions))
- **ctrl+r** searches prompt history; in fullscreen ctrl+s cycles its scope (session, project, everywhere).
- **/resume** picker has `/` search by name, summary or PR URL; **/export** writes the conversation to a file.
- **Mods** (plugins with JavaScript): can draw panes beside the transcript or bands above the prompt, redraw tool rows and dialogs, add commands; cannot change scrolling directly. ([mods](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview.md))
- Transcripts are JSONL under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/`, but the format is internal and changes between versions; stable inputs are `/export`, `claude -p --resume <id> --output-format json`, and hooks' `transcript_path`.

**Does the module attach after `/reload-plugins`?** Yes, by the host's contract. `hooks/hooks.json` lists `register.tsx` under `modules`, and its `on('tool.call', { tool: 'TaskCreate' }, ...)` hooks join the chain whenever the module loads, at startup or at a reload. `session.start` also fires once per fresh load of a plugin, a reload included, so the tools register and `hydrate()` runs then too. The only time this was seen was the mid-session swap from 0.1.0 (Python command hooks) to 2.0.0 (a function-hooks module); in later sessions the module was running, as the SessionStart reminder showed. That upgrade path doesn't recur, and I can't reproduce it from 2.0.0 onward.

**Does numbering continue after a resume?** Yes, while the session id is the same. Counters, the `created` map, the ledger and the `closed` rulings are stored under `session:<sid>`, and `hydrate()` raises the counters to the stored ones and to every label it finds (`coverLabels`), so the next label continues from the highest even if the task files are gone. The transcripts on this machine keep one session id per file across resumes. If a resume does change the session id while `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` keeps the task list, the stored record comes back empty; #18 keeps items already in plugin state across that, and [lokkju/skills#26](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/26) is the work to key the record by the task list id. Ruling (2026-10-14): yes. New repos that aren't Rust crates use yeet, for SemVer as well as CalVer. Rust crates stay on release-plz. yeet already releases the CalVer repos (codexpublicus/gorsuch-library and this repo). Before the forge-release skill (#11) makes yeet the SemVer default, one public repo now on release-please (lokkju/dbxdebug or lokkju/git-spreader) moves to yeet as a pilot, and the pilot checks how yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the package's own version.

What I established before changing anything, on Claude Code 2.1.286.

**How I checked.** A throwaway function-hooks plugin, loaded with `--plugin-dir` under `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1`, logged `$.session.id()`, `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID`, the store's keys and the `classic.SessionStart` input into its own `$.store`, across `claude -p` runs that created tasks with TaskCreate. The runs started inside a background job, so I unset the job's own variables (`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION`, `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_JOB_DIR`, the messaging socket) for each child; anything else the job sets was inherited. For the background-job path I read the engine's bundled code and the files the #9 incident left behind, since a headless run can't background itself.

**(a) `--resume` and `--continue` keep the session id.** `--resume <id>` and `--continue` both came back as the original id, and TaskList in each showed the tasks from the earlier runs (one task list, `~/.claude/tasks/<id>`). `--resume <id> --fork-session` got a new id and an empty task list (`source: fork`).

One wrinkle: under `--continue`, `$.session.id()` read inside the `classic.SessionStart` hook returned a throwaway id, not the resumed one; the hook input's `session_id` was correct, and `$.session.id()` was right again by `session.start`. So the plugin's post-resume `hydrate()` reads the wrong store record and the wrong task directory on `--continue`.

**(b) Backgrounding a session forks it, and the fork gets a copy of the task list.** The engine's background fork (`forkSessionToBackground`, which prints "Your conversation was backgrounded, resume it with: claude --resume <forkSessionId>") gives the job a new session id, rewrites the transcript under it, and then runs a "carry to fork" step: when `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` is unset and the list is the session's own, it copies every file from `tasks/<old id>` into `tasks/<new id>`, best effort with a 2-second cap. With `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` set, it copies nothing and both sessions share that list.

That is exactly what happened in #9. Session `b54339de` was backgrounded on 2026-10-13 at 02:03:40 as job `3eb3b414`: `tasks/3eb3b414-…` holds the same 31 task files, 113 to 143, written at 02:03:40; the 24 that neither session touched afterwards are still byte-identical, and the other 7 keep their task ids and D/A labels with revised subjects. The job's timeline starts eight seconds later. The plugin store still holds `session:b54339de-…` with the ledger A38, A39 and A40 and counters D78/A40, and `session:3eb3b414-…` with D94/A56 and an empty ledger. `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` was not set. So the ledger didn't vanish from the store; the new session id just never looked at the old record.

A job restarted by the daemon is a different case: the job directory is named for the session id, and this job (`be9a7ddd`, with an `exit-cause` of `cli_error` from an earlier death) is still running as session `be9a7ddd-…` on the same task list. I didn't force a restart to watch it happen.

**(c) Compaction keeps the session id and the task list.** `/compact` on a resumed run fired `classic.SessionStart` with `source: compact` under the same id, and the task files were untouched. The #9 transcript also shows a compaction inside one session id.

**`$.store`** is one JSON file per installed plugin (`~/.claude/plugins/store/<plugin>_<marketplace>-<hash>.json`), shared by every session, so it persisted through all of the above. A `--plugin-dir` copy gets a file of its own.

**What follows for the fix.** Keying by `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` covers a shared list (where it's set, a fork keeps the list and changes the session id), so I'm doing that, with the migration. It doesn't cover #9, because there the list id is the session id and changes with it. For that case a session with no record of its own, whose task files show decision items, adopts the record of the stored session whose task directory holds those same task ids with the same labels (labels survive a revision; subjects don't): the session it was forked from. And the `classic.SessionStart` hook will hydrate with the hook input's `session_id` instead of `$.session.id()`.

What I established before changing anything, on Claude Code 2.1.286.

**How I checked.** A throwaway function-hooks plugin, loaded with `--plugin-dir` under `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1`, logged the names `$.tool.list()` returned at `session.start`, `classic.SessionStart` and before and after every `tool.call`, plus each `tool.describe` event with its `isDeferred`. The headless run (`claude -p --model sonnet`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`) made the model run Bash, then `ToolSearch` with `select:TaskCreate,TaskUpdate`, then TaskCreate, then Bash again. A control run without `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS` made one Bash call. As in #26, I unset the background job's own variables for each child.

**`$.tool.list()` includes deferred tools.** With the task tools enabled, `tool.describe` fired for TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskStop and TaskUpdate with `isDeferred: true`, and `$.tool.list()` returned all five at `session.start` and before the first Bash call, when nothing had been loaded through ToolSearch yet. The list was the same 256 names before and after the ToolSearch call; loading a tool doesn't change it. So the list is the tools that exist in the session, not the ones whose schemas the model has loaded. (The plugin's own `decision_add` and `decision_close` are deferred the same way and listed the same way.)

**The control discriminates.** Without `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS`, the list had TaskStop and ToolSearch but no TaskCreate, TaskList, TaskGet or TaskUpdate. So `decision_close`'s check from #18 refuses a task-list item exactly when TaskUpdate exists, loaded or not, and settles it in the queue when TaskUpdate doesn't exist. The failure this issue worried about doesn't happen on this build.

**The declarations don't say either way.** `ToolInfo` is `{ name, description, mcp }` with no deferred flag, and `$.tool.list()` is described as "the tools the model can call now", which a deferred tool is (by name, after ToolSearch). The only deferral API is the `tool.describe` event; there's no call that lists deferred or loaded tools.

**One aside.** In the headless run, `$.tool.list()` inside `classic.SessionStart` threw ("no session is bound in this process"). `decision_close` only calls it from a tool call, where it worked every time, and the plugin's check already treats a throw as "TaskUpdate isn't offered".

**What follows.** No change to the check. I'm adding a test that pins this (TaskUpdate deferred and never loaded still makes `decision_close` and `decision_update` point at TaskUpdate), making those refusals say that TaskUpdate may need loading through ToolSearch first, and noting the dependency in the README's Limits, since nothing in the declarations promises it.

The subagent question, checked on Claude Code 2.1.286 with session-decisions 2026.10.15.1.

**How I checked.** Four headless runs (`claude -p --model sonnet`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`) with the installed plugin plus a throwaway probe plugin loaded through `--plugin-dir`. The probe logged `$.session.id()`, `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID`, `$.agent.list()` and the loop's `agentId` at every TaskCreate and decision tool `tool.call`, plus the classic `PostToolUse` and `SubagentStart` inputs' `session_id` and `agent_id`. As in #25 and #26, I unset the background job's own variables for each child. Limits: headless only, one build, general-purpose subagents only; no interactive session, teammate or workflow agent.

**Foreground subagent: same session, same hooks, same list.** The parent's TaskCreate came back as D1 and the subagent's as D2, so the subagent's call went through the plugin's TaskCreate hook on the same counter. In both, `$.session.id()` was the parent's session id; the subagent's `tool.call` carried `agentId` set to its loop's id (absent on the parent's), and the classic `PostToolUse` input had the parent's `session_id` with the subagent's `agent_id` and `agent_type`. `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` was unset in both. Both task files (`1.json`, `2.json`) landed in `~/.claude/tasks/<parent session id>/`. So a foreground subagent's items are in the list ctrl+t shows.

**Background subagent: no task tools.** With `run_in_background: true`, the subagent had neither TaskCreate nor TaskUpdate, even with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` (ToolSearch found neither). It fell back to `decision_add`, which came back as D2 after the parent's D1: same session id, same queue, same counter. TaskList in the parent then showed only D1, so the subagent's item is a ledger item that ctrl+t doesn't show, while the cards, sidebar and `/decisions` should (I didn't render them headless). That's the failure the original note predicted, for background subagents only, and the plugin handles it the way it handles any session without task tools; the README doesn't mention that a background subagent is such a case.

**One real bug.** A background subagent can't settle a task-list item. `decision_close` decides from `$.tool.list()`, and inside the subagent's call that list named TaskUpdate (the main loop's tools), so it refused D1 and pointed at TaskUpdate, which the subagent doesn't have. Filed as [lokkju/skills#37](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/37), with the README gap.

That answers the question this issue left open, so I'm closing it; the remaining work is #37.

Pilot status: lokkju/dbxdebug is the pilot repo; [lokkju/dbxdebug#26](https://github.com/lokkju/dbxdebug/pull/26) moves it to yeet v0.17.0 with `versioning: semver`, and [lokkju/infra#259](https://github.com/lokkju/infra/pull/259) gives it the release App's credentials. Neither is merged.

I picked dbxdebug over git-spreader because it released three times in September (git-spreader last released in May), it has a second version file for yeet to manage (`plugin.json`, which release-please never bumped and which has sat at 0.1.0 through five releases), and its publish path has a `workflow_dispatch` recovery job worth carrying over. Neither repo's `uv.lock` records its own version: both get it from hatch-vcs.

The `uv.lock` question, checked on a scratch copy of dbxdebug: with a static `version = "0.5.0" # x-yeet-version`, `uv lock` writes `version = "0.5.0"` into the package's lock entry, and bumping pyproject to 0.6.0 the way a yeet release PR would makes `uv sync --locked` and `uv lock --check` fail. yeet's `version_files` can't fix that (uv rewrites `uv.lock` and drops comment markers). With hatch-vcs's dynamic version, uv writes no version line for the project, so the release PR leaves the lock valid. For SemVer yeet on a uv project, the forge-release and python-project skills should require hatch-vcs.

Two settings release-please users will trip on: yeet's pre-1.0 default bumps patch for a feat, so matching release-please's `bump-patch-for-minor-pre-major: false` needs `pre_major_features_bump_patch: false`; and the publish job has to stay in the file PyPI's Trusted Publisher names, now triggered by `release: published`, since yeet sets no step outputs for an in-run publish.

The dry run against origin/main found v0.5.0 as the current version and nothing to release yet.

Rulings on the design questions (2026-10-15):

- **GraphQL (Q3):** allowed. POST goes only to the GraphQL endpoint, and only for documents whose operations are all queries, checked by parsing the operation type rather than matching a string. #21's "GET-only" meant read-only.
- **Write wrapper (Q4):** the wrapper does the write itself: `<wrapper> <op>`, JSON on stdin, and a non-zero exit refuses.
- **Agent-ready (Q5):** as proposed: open, not person-only and not blocked. The agent label only sorts items within a tier.
- **Rulings and needs-human (Q6):** yes. Recording a ruling adds decision-made and removes needs-human and decision in one step.
- **Prototype (Q2):** not needed. Its lessons are already in #24 and in this doc. A local test instance replaces it.
- **Still open:** Q1 (Python CLI or TypeScript), Q7 (closing references; being revised to "expect one only when the work came from an issue, and warn"), Q8 (test setup; proposing a docker-compose stack of Forgejo and GitLab CE with recorded fixtures for CI) and Q9 (merged-but-open).

The remaining rulings (2026-10-15). Every question in the doc is now settled:

- **Architecture (Q1):** a standard-library Python CLI plus a thin hooks module. `$.http.fetch` can't pin a CA, `$.fs.write` can't set 0600 or write atomically, and agents can't call slash commands.
- **Closing references (Q7, revised):** `Closes #N` is expected only when the work was picked up from an issue, recorded by forge-tracker or named in the branch. A missing one only warns, and PRs with no issue are untouched.
- **Test setup (Q8):** a docker-compose stack of Forgejo and GitLab CE, with a seed script for repos, issues, MRs, labels and blocking links. Fixtures recorded from it keep CI fast, live runs go against the stack on ml-01, and GitHub uses a dedicated test repo created through infra Pulumi.
- **Merged but open (Q9):** propose a close only for real closing references. An `#N` seen only in a title or branch goes to the unclear bucket.

Draft design for the forge-tracker plugin in `docs/specs/forge-tracker.md`. No code.

It covers [#12](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/12) (the plugin and its fixed constraints), [#21](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/21) (read-only forge layer for GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo), [#22](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/22) (`/groom`), [#23](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/23) (`/catchup`) and [#24](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/24) (`/next`): detection, the normalized reads, three-valued mergeability per #24's comment, the separate write path and write-wrapper, config, each command with example output, the working-rule skill, the SessionStart list and `Closes #N` hook, state, independence, testing, and a phased plan starting with the GitHub read layer and `/catchup`.

The prototype #24's comment mentions wasn't found from ml-01 (GitHub code search across lokkju and codexpublicus, local repos and their history, ~/.claude, ~/.cache); the doc's "The prototype" section lists where I looked.

Nine open questions, each with a recommendation, are at the end of the doc under "Questions for Loki".

Redesigns two parts of the session-decisions cards (context: [lokkju/skills#20](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/20)). This replaces the inline More/Less expansion added in [lokkju/skills#32](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/32).

**More as a dialog.** More, or a press on the card's label, calls `$.ui.ask` with the item's label as the header. The question text is the item's question, the full recommendation when the `recommends` tag shortens it, and the description as plain text, cut to six lines and 320 characters. Options, at most four: `Accept: <choice>` for a decision or `Done` for an action, `Copy link` for an http(s) link, `Copy <first command>` for the first code span, and `Close`. Accept and Done fill the same prompt lines as the card's buttons; text typed under Other fills `<label>: <text>` through `mergeAnswers`; a dismissed dialog does nothing. The `expanded` atom, the Less state and the inline detail block are gone.

**Link line.** `#N`, `!N`, `owner/repo#N` and `no link` stay at the right of the button row. Anything else moves to its own line under the question and qualifier: a `Link` labelled `owner/repo#N` for GitHub issue and pull request URLs, `owner/repo` for repository URLs, and the URL itself otherwise, inside a `wrap="wrap"` Text so nothing is truncated. A link `Link` can't take (plain `http:` other than localhost) is dim wrapped text.

**Tests.** The test engine fakes `AskUserQuestion` (what `$.ui.ask` calls) with scripted replies or a dismissal. New tests cover the dialog's header, question and options, Accept, Done, typed text, Close, dismissal, both copy options, the description cut, the link line for GitHub, long and plain-http URLs, `#N` staying on the button row, and the absence of any inline detail block; `githubShort`, `isShortLink` and `excerpt` have unit tests. The old More/Less test is replaced.

Not verified: how the real dialog draws a multi-line question. The question is kept to the question, one recommendation line and a short description excerpt for that reason.

The forge-release skill's decision tree currently routes CalVer (and anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps) to yeet, SemVer packages on GitHub to release-please, and Rust crates to release-plz. The question is whether the middle branch should go to yeet too, so one tool covers every non-crate repo. The python-project skill's release-please default would follow whatever this decides.

## The case for keeping release-please, checked

- **Native version files.** Weaker than it sounds. Neither tool updates `uv.lock`: release-please has googleapis/release-please#2561 open for it. yeet updates `pyproject.toml` through a marker comment (`version = "1.2.3" # x-yeet-version`) and `package.json` through `json_pointer: /version`, which covers the files these repos publish from.
- **Tokens.** No difference. Both run on `GITHUB_TOKEN` when the publish step lives in the release workflow, and both need a GitHub App token only when the release has to start another workflow (one of my sites' deploy does).
- **Maturity.** The real one. yeet (monkescience/yeet, MIT) was created in February 2026 and has 4 contributors and 7 stars; release-please is Google's and widely used.
- **Language plugins.** release-please has strategies and plugins for Java, Ruby, PHP, Helm and node or cargo workspaces. None of these repos use them.

## Why the maturity risk is small here

- yeet runs as a container pinned by digest, so an abandoned yeet keeps working at the pinned version.
- Its only state is git tags and `CHANGELOG.md`, both tool-agnostic, so leaving it is a config swap. yeet's docs carry a migrate-from-release-please guide, and the reverse is the same shape.
- Telemetry is on by default; the skill already sets `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

## What standardizing gets

One tool, one `.yeet.yaml` shape and one App pattern across GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps, for CalVer and SemVer. The skill's decision tree drops a branch, and its references drop the release-please setup and troubleshooting.

## Proposal

- New repos: yeet, SemVer or CalVer.
- Rust crates: release-plz stays. It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't.
- Repos on release-please today move only when someone is in them anyway: lokkju/dbxdebug, lokkju/git-spreader and two private repos. release-plz today: lokkju/neovision and two private repos.
- python-project switches its release default to yeet.

## Not yet checked

- How yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the project's own version (a release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml` but not `uv.lock` would fail `uv sync --locked`). release-please has the same gap; the usual fixes are a dynamic version (hatch-vcs) or a follow-up `uv lock` commit on the release branch.
- yeet's monorepo targets against release-please's linked versions, if a multi-package repo ever needs them.
response.title: forge-release: standardize on yeet for new repos instead of release-please for SemVer on GitHub?

These findings are against 0.1.0, the Python version; 2.x is a TypeScript rewrite, so check which still apply before working on them.

Seven minor findings from the final review of session-decisions 0.1.0, deferred at ship time. The first two are worth fixing in the next pass; the rest are polish.

1. **Any trailing bracket counts as the link** (`scripts/session_decisions/subject.py`, `_LINK`). `ACTION: press [Enter]` is accepted with `[Enter]` as its link. Check the token against the forms the skill lists: `#N`, `!N`, `owner/repo#N`, a URL, or `no link`.
2. **Other self-numbering forms bypass the hook** (`subject.py`, `_DRAFT`). `D7: DECIDE: ...`, `[D7] DECIDE: ...` and `D7 - DECIDE: ...` don't match, so they go through unlabelled and unchecked. Widen the optional label prefix (something like `[\[(]?[DA]\d+[\])]?[\s:.-]*`).
3. **The flock wait has no deadline** (`store.py`, `SessionState.locked`). A blocking `LOCK_EX` runs into the hook's 10s timeout; since the 0.1.0 fix the item then shows as `D?` rather than vanishing. A `LOCK_NB` retry loop with a ~5s deadline, then fail open, would be cleaner.
4. **`/decisions statusline` path** (`commands/decisions.md`). If command text isn't substituted, the model has no real path to show. Substitution worked on 2.1.284, so this is defensive: a `decisions.py where` subcommand would remove the dependency.
5. **Concurrency is tested at the store level only** (`tests/test_store.py`). Add a test that runs two `hook-pretooluse` processes at once.
6. **Items with no recorded creation time sort first** (`store.py`, `all_items`). Cosmetic.
7. **Shared task lists** (`paths.py`, `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID`). The lock and counter are per session but the list is shared, so two sessions writing at once can collide. Document in the README's Limits.

Also open from the review: whether subagent hook payloads carry the parent's `session_id` and share its task list. Worth one headless check; if not, a subagent's items land in a queue ctrl+t doesn't show.

Found while settling the last question on [lokkju/skills#13](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/13), on Claude Code 2.1.286 in headless `claude -p` runs with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, session-decisions 2026.10.15.1 installed.

**What happens.** The parent creates D1 with TaskCreate. A background subagent (`Agent` with `run_in_background: true`) is told the user answered D1 and to settle it. The subagent has no TaskUpdate: it isn't in its tool list and `ToolSearch` `select:TaskUpdate` answers "No matching deferred tools found". So it calls `decision_close`, which refuses:

> session-decisions: D1 is a task-list item; mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description. If TaskUpdate is deferred, load it with ToolSearch first.

The ruling is recorded nowhere and the task file stays pending. `decision_update` goes through the same `TaskUpdate` check, so I'd expect it to dead-end the same way (not run).

**Why.** `taskUpdateOffered()` in `hooks/register.tsx` asks `$.tool.list()`. A probe hook logged that list inside the subagent's `decision_close` call (the `tool.call` event carried the subagent's `agentId`), and it named TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskStop and TaskUpdate: the main loop's tools, not the subagent's. The declaration says "the tools the model can call now", which isn't what it returned for a subagent's loop.

**Related, documentation only.** A background subagent gets no TaskCreate either, so its items go through `decision_add` and are ledger items: they share the parent's queue and counter (the subagent's item came back as D2 after the parent's D1) but never appear in ctrl+t, even though the parent's do. The README's "Without them" paragraph and the ctrl+t limit describe a session with no task tools; they don't cover a session whose background subagents lack them. A foreground subagent does get TaskCreate, and its items land in the parent's task list with the parent's labels.

The fix is the maintainer's call; options I can see are deciding from the loop (`e.agentId` is set on a subagent's `tool.call`, and `$.agent.list()` lists the loop by that id, though it has no background flag), or letting `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the call comes from a subagent.
response.title: session-decisions: decision_close dead-ends in a background subagent ($.tool.list() reports the parent's TaskUpdate)

Follow-up from #18, which fixes #9.

## What #18 assumes

`decision_close` now settles a task-list item only when TaskUpdate isn't in the session's tool list. It checks that with `$.tool.list()`, which the engine's declarations describe as "the tools the model can call now". Nobody has checked whether that list includes a **deferred** tool the model hasn't loaded through ToolSearch yet. TaskCreate, TaskList, TaskUpdate and TaskGet are deferred in the sessions that have them.

If `$.tool.list()` leaves deferred tools out, `decision_close` accepts a task-list item even though TaskUpdate exists. The item shows as settled in the queue, but its task file stays open, so ctrl+t and the task list disagree with the queue.

## What to do

1. Find out what `$.tool.list()` returns for a deferred tool. Check the engine's type declarations (run `/plugin-types` in Claude Code to write them for the current build) and the test harness. If neither settles it, check a real session: load the plugin with `--plugin-dir` in a background or `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` session, where the task tools exist but are deferred, and log what `$.tool.list()` returns.
2. If deferred tools are missing, make the check see them. Use whatever the engine offers for deferred or known tools. Failing that, treat TaskUpdate as available whenever TaskCreate is known to have run in the session.
3. Add a test for the deferred case in `tests/register.test.tsx`.

## Where to start

`plugins/session-decisions/hooks/register.tsx`, the `decision_close` handler. #18 adds the `$.tool.list()` call. If #18 isn't merged when you start, branch from `fix/sd-tools-gap` and say in the PR that it's stacked on #18.

Fixes #26.

The facts behind this are in [the issue comment](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/26#issuecomment-6180088351). In short: `--resume`, `--continue` and compaction keep the session id; backgrounding a session forks it under a new id and copies its task files into `tasks/<new id>` (unless `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` is set, when nothing is copied and the list is shared). That is what happened in #9: `session:b54339de-…` in the store still holds A38 to A40, and the backgrounded job `3eb3b414` read its own, empty record.

**Changes, in `hooks/register.tsx`:**
- **Forks.** A session with no record whose task files hold decision items adopts the record of the stored session whose task list holds every one of those items by task id and label, with at least one word for word; the most recently used one wins. The fork gets a copy, and the parent keeps its own.
- **Shared task lists.** With `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` set, the record is `list:<id>`. A `session:<sid>` record for the same session moves under it on the first read. `persist` merges with what's stored, keeping the higher counters, every creation time and every ledger item (the settled copy wins), so two sessions on one list don't erase each other's ledger.
- **`prune`** keeps the 100 most recently used records across both key kinds.
- **`--continue`.** `$.session.id()` read in `classic.SessionStart` returns a placeholder id under `--continue`, while the hook input's `session_id` is right. The resume hook now hydrates with `e.session_id`.

**Tests:** seven new cases in `tests/register.test.tsx`: the list-keyed record and concurrent writes to it, a new session id on the same list keeping counters, ledger and rulings, migration of an old session record, a fork adopting its parent's record (and not a stranger whose list has the same ids and labels), a fresh session adopting nothing, the resume hook using the input's id, and prune across both key kinds. Six of them fail against `main`. The test engine now keeps several task lists and its own in-memory store, so a test can seed what an earlier process left. `claude plugin test`: 53 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict` and `tsc` pass.

**Not verified:** a real background fork against this plugin (it can't be triggered headless; the behaviour comes from the engine's code and the #9 files), and a daemon restart of a job, which on the evidence of the job directories keeps its session id.

Follow-up from #18, which fixes #9.

## What isn't proven

In #9, ledger items A38 to A40 vanished when the task tools came back. #18 fixes the merge in `hydrate()`, so items in plugin state and the stored record survive a re-read of the task files. Why the stored record lacked those items in the first place is unproven.

The likeliest cause: the session resumed under a **new session id** while `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` kept the old task list. The plugin keys its stored record by session id (`session:<sid>` in `$.store`), so the resumed session read an empty record. #18's second register test simulates that, but nobody has confirmed it against a real resume.

1. Confirm what happens to the session id and the plugin store across a resume, a `/exit` and restart of a background job, and a compaction. If the id changes, find whether `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` or the tasks directory stays stable.
2. If the id changes while the task list stays, key the stored record (counters, the `created` map, the ledger, the `closed` rulings) by the task list id when one is set, and fall back to the session id otherwise. Migrate an existing `session:<sid>` record the first time.
3. Add tests for a resume with a new session id and the same task list, plus the migration.
4. Update the README's "How it stays in sync" and "Limits" sections.

`plugins/session-decisions/hooks/register.tsx`: `loadRecord`, `persist`, `prune` and `hydrate`. If #18 isn't merged when you start, branch from `fix/sd-tools-gap` and say in the PR that it's stacked on #18.

The session-decisions queue shows item subjects as raw text, but the subjects are written in markdown: backticks around commands and paths, `**bold**`, and `[text](url)` links. In the list they render as literal backticks, asterisks and brackets, which makes long items (many are 300+ characters) hard to read.

- **Or strip it** for the list view (drop the backticks and asterisks, show link text only) and keep the raw text for copying.

The skill and README treat TaskCreate as the normal path and the `decision_add`/`decision_close` ledger as a rare fallback. Several sessions on Claude Code 2.1.286 didn't get TaskCreate at all:

| Session | How it was launched | Task tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| interactive, `--model sonnet` (the demo recorder) | from a normal terminal, inside tmux, with `--settings`, `--plugin-dir` and `--permission-mode default` | TaskStop only; `ToolSearch select:TaskCreate` returned "No matching deferred tools found" |
| `claude -p --model sonnet` | from inside a background job (inherits its environment) | TaskStop only |
| `claude -p --model opus` | from inside a background job | TaskStop only |
| `claude -p --model haiku` | from inside a background job | TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate, TaskStop |
| a background job on Opus | Claude Code background session | TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate (deferred) |
| the user's own interactive sessions | normal | have the side panel with task-list items |

**What gates it is unknown.** The `-p` probes all ran inside a background job, so they can't separate the model from the launch environment. The tool list adds the four task tools whenever `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS` isn't explicitly false, so something downstream filters them.

- **Cards:** the `ledger` tag reads as an error to someone who never sees the other path.

_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#7._

Related: #7 covers the hook half (a TaskUpdate subject losing its label).

**Problem:** the session-decisions skill says how to create an item and how to close it with a ruling. It says nothing about revising an open item when its context or recommendation changes, so the queue goes stale.

**Example from a session (2026-10-05):** D27 was created as "serve the data bundle as `application/x-protobuf` so Cloudflare compresses it (recommend accept)". The user answered with a question, not a ruling: "any other way to force it to be compressed that doesn't lie about the contents quite so much?" Claude replied with new options and a changed recommendation (a pre-gzipped `.bin.gz` served as `application/gzip`, decompressed with DecompressionStream), but only in chat. The D27 item, and so the decisions pane, still showed the old question and recommendation until the user pointed it out.

**What the skill should say:** a section like "When an open item changes", covering:
- **A follow-up question or a partial answer isn't a ruling.** Leave the item open and revise it.
- **When the options, the recommendation, the question or the context change,** TaskUpdate the item's subject (keeping its `D<n>`/`A<n>` label, with the recommendation and link in the same format the hook validates) and its description in the same turn as the chat reply.
- **Append rather than overwrite:** add `Revised (<YYYY-MM-DD>): <what changed and why>` to the description, so the history of what the user was shown survives.
- **A different question:** if the answer turns it into a different question, complete the old item as `Ruling (<date>): superseded by D<m>` and create a new one, instead of silently repurposing the label.

**Plugin side:**
- `hooks/subject.ts`: check that the subject validation also runs on TaskUpdate subject changes, not only TaskCreate, so a revised subject keeps its recommendation and link.
- **Fallback ledger:** it has `decision_add` and `decision_close` but no update. Add `decision_update` (label, new text and/or description) so fallback mode can revise too.
- **The pane:** consider marking revised items (e.g. "revised" with the date) so the user notices the recommendation changed.
- **Tests:** a revised subject that drops the recommendation is rejected; a revision keeps the label and appends `Revised (...)`; `decision_update` in fallback mode.

The TaskCreate hook rejected this subject with "a DECIDE item needs a recommendation, written as (recommend <choice>)":

```
DECIDE: what to work on next in lokkju/skills? (recommend: ship release #16 now, then a session-decisions hardening release (#14 rest, #4 skill wording, #20, triage #15 and #13), then settle #10 and write the forge-release skill #11, then forge-tracker) [https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues]
```

At the time it looked like the nested parenthetical was the cause. It isn't: `CHOICE` in `hooks/subject.ts` already allows one nested level, and this body without the colon passes `problems()` and yields the full choice from `recommendation()`. The cause is the colon in `(recommend: ...`. `RECOMMEND` is `/\(recommend\s+\S/i`, so `(recommend:` never matches, and the error message doesn't say so.

Two things to fix:

- Accept `(recommend: <choice>)` as well as `(recommend <choice>)` in `problems()`, `recommendation()` and `splitBody()`. Models write the colon form naturally.
- `recommendation()` and `splitBody()` handle one level of nesting only. A choice with two nested levels passes validation but loses its Accept button and its recommends tag. Matching the closing parenthesis by depth instead of by regex removes the limit.

Fixes #27.

The rejected subject in #27 was written as `(recommend: ...)`. The hook's check required whitespace right after `recommend`, so the colon form failed; the nested parenthetical was already handled. This change:

- accepts `(recommend: <choice>)` alongside `(recommend <choice>)` in `problems()`, `recommendation()` and `splitBody()`;
- finds the end of the recommendation by parenthesis depth, so a choice nested two or more levels deep keeps its Accept button and tag (the old regex allowed one level);
- cuts the card's short tag at the first comma or semicolon outside parentheses, so `B (cheaper, faster)` isn't split mid-parenthetical.

An unclosed `(recommend yes` still passes validation as before, but offers no Accept choice.

Tests: the subject from #27 in both spellings at the unit level, deeper nesting, the short tag, and a TaskCreate-to-Accept test through the hook. Both new tests fail on `main`.

## What happens

After a session resumes (here: the user ran `/exit` and the background job restarted), the harness no longer offers `TaskCreate`, `TaskGet`, `TaskList` or `TaskUpdate`, but the session-decisions queue still lists the task-list items created before the restart. Those items can't be settled any more:

- `TaskUpdate` isn't available, so the documented way to close a task-list item is gone.
- `decision_close` refuses them: `session-decisions: A37 isn't in the fallback ledger. If it's a task-list item, mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description.`

So a finished item (A37 here) keeps showing in the SessionStart reminder ("Open items in this session's decision queue, still waiting on the user") and in the UI, and the user reasonably asks why it's still open.

New items in the same session correctly fall back to `decision_add` (they get ledger labels, e.g. A38, A39), so the labels keep counting; only closing pre-restart task-list items is stuck.

## Repro

1. In a background session with task tools, create an ACTION item via TaskCreate (gets A37).
2. Restart the session so the task tools are no longer offered (resume after `/exit` in a background job).
3. Try to close it: `decision_close` with label A37 is refused; no TaskUpdate exists.

## Suggested fix

Either:
- let `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the task tools aren't available (record the ruling in the plugin's own store and mark the item closed there, so the reminder and UI stop listing it; reconcile if TaskUpdate comes back), or
- have the SessionStart reminder and UI read the task list's real status and drop items the harness can no longer update, with a note.

The first keeps "every hand-off is a queue item" working across restarts. A test: create via the tasks source, simulate no task tools, close via `decision_close`, expect the item closed and absent from the reminder.

Related: [lokkju/skills#7](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/7) (TaskUpdate subject edits dropping labels).

Stacked on [lokkju/skills#17](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/17): this branch starts from it, so its first commit shows here until #17 merges. Review the last two commits.

Design: [comment on #9](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/9#issuecomment-6136779661).

- `decision_close` settles a task-list item when `$.tool.list()` has no TaskUpdate (or the host can't list tools). The item is marked completed with the usual `Ruling (<date>): ...` line in plugin state, and a copy goes into a new `closed` map in the session's store record, keyed by task id. While TaskUpdate is offered, task items are still refused with a pointer to it, so the task file gets updated when it can be. The "not found" deny now fires only for a label that is nowhere in the queue: `session-decisions: D9 isn't in this session's decision queue.`
- `hydrate()` merges through a pure `mergeHydrated()` instead of replacing: ledger items are the stored ledger plus those already in state (state wins), a stored ruling overrides a task file that still shows its item open, and a settled item whose task file has gone stays settled.
- A later TaskUpdate that sets the task's status drops the stored ruling, since the task file has the status then.
- Ledger items made while the task tools were missing stay ledger items and stay closable with `decision_close`.
- README ("How it stays in sync", "Limits") and SKILL.md describe what happens when the tools come and go, including that ctrl+t still shows an item settled this way as pending.

Tests: `mergeHydrated()` and `settle()` in `tests/queue.test.ts`. In `tests/register.test.tsx`, closing a task item is refused while TaskUpdate is offered, then settles it once the tool list is empty, the task file stays pending, the resume reminder leaves it out and `/decisions all` shows it completed with its ruling, and unknown labels are still refused. A second test resumes under a new session id with the same `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID`, so the store record comes back empty, and checks that the ledger item and the stored ruling survive, and that the ledger item closes with `decision_close` after the tools return. 28 pass; `tsc` and `claude plugin validate --strict` are clean.

The cause of the vanished ledger in #9 isn't proven. `hydrate()` already read the stored ledger, so the record it read must have lacked A38 to A40; a resume that changed the session id while the task list id held fits that, and is what the second test simulates. The merge covers it when plugin state survives the resume. If state doesn't survive either, keying the store record by the task list id would be the next step; this PR doesn't do that.

Fixes #9

## What happens

When a decision item's subject is changed with `TaskUpdate` and the new subject is written the way the skill tells the assistant to write subjects (`DECIDE: ... (recommend X) [link]`, no label), the task ends up with no `D<N>`/`A<N>` label. The task list then shows items like `DECIDE: approve the agent dispatcher spec ...` with no number, and the queue can't refer to them.

Seen in an infra session on 2026-10-10/11: five items (D65, A24, D71, D72, D73) lost their labels after their questions were revised per the "revise open decisions" practice.

## Why

`hooks/register.tsx`, the `TaskUpdate` handler, runs `next(e)` with `e.subject` unchanged and only then mirrors the change with `applyUpdate`. The `TaskCreate` handler rewrites the subject to add the label before the tool runs; the `TaskUpdate` handler has no equivalent, so the stored task subject is the unlabelled draft. In `hooks/queue.ts`, `applyUpdate` then reparses the new subject with `itemFromTask`, which (for an unlabelled draft) either drops the item or rebuilds it without its label.

## Suggested fix

In the `TaskUpdate` handler, before `next(e)`: if `e.subject` parses as a draft (`parseDraft`) and the task is an existing item, rewrite `e.subject` to `formatSubject(current.label, draft)`, keeping the item's label (and refuse a kind change, or allow it with a new label). Also run `problems(draft)` so a revised DECIDE still needs a recommendation and a link. A test in `tests/queue.test.ts` for "update with an unlabelled draft keeps the label".

The SKILL.md could also say that a revised subject keeps its label, though the hook fixing it is better than relying on the assistant.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Like `/catchup`, it can ship for one forge first.

**`/next`** recommends what to work on: the user's own queue, work agents can start now, and what is blocked. It is read-only. It recommends, and never claims, assigns, comments or branches.

**Two layers, both cached outside the repo** under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/next/<host>_<project>/`:
1. **Facts (a script).**
   - **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state; branches with no PR/MR.
   - **How it caches:** under a fingerprint of cheap inputs. These are the default-branch head, the newest issue, PR and pipeline `updated_at`, open issue and PR counts, a digest of the milestones (id, title, due date), the remote branch heads, and a schema tag that hashes the code itself. When the fingerprint is unchanged, the cached facts are reused, so a rerun takes seconds. A run with a failed read is written but never reused.
2. **The slate (Claude's ranking).** It is stored with the facts' fingerprint and shown again unchanged until the fingerprint moves.
   - **The user's queue:** person-only items, ordered by how many agent-ready items each one unblocks, counted transitively through blocking links and cycle-safe.
   - **Agent lanes:** unblocked agent-ready items by tier and due date, grouped into lanes that shouldn't touch the same files. The grouping is a stated judgement, not a measurement. A lane that already has an open PR or a pushed branch is marked in flight.
   - **Blocked:** each blocked item and what it waits on.

**Classification rules learned the hard way:**
- **What person-only means:** the configured decision or needs-human labels, plus configurable keyword markers (e.g. hardware, legal).
- **Not person-only:** an assignee is never a reason, because agents share the user's account. Show the assignee as an owner. Some markers are only hints Claude may overrule; design work an agent can build is one example.
- **Merged-but-open issues inflate the ready list badly.** Flag issues that a merged PR/MR references but that are still open. That check, and fixing it, belongs to `/groom` (#22).

**Future enhancement, not now:** a status pane that shows the slate's top items, its age and a "stale" flag when the fingerprint moves. It reads only the cache, and shares a display mechanism with the session-decisions pane.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Each command can ship for one forge first, but the layer is what makes it work on GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo alike.

**`/catchup`** is for coming back to a project after time away: what changed, and what is waiting on you. It is read-only: no claims, comments or merges.

**The window:**
- It starts where the user's previous successful `/catchup` ended, kept in a local marker. **Not** at "your last forge activity": agents act under the user's account, and in practice that gives a four-minute window opening at an agent's last push.
- The marker lives under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/catchup/<host>_<project>_<user>.json`. The directory is 0700 and files 0600, writes are atomic, and a relative XDG value is ignored.
- The next window starts a few minutes before the marker, so a fast local clock can't skip events. Seeing an event twice is harmless.
- The marker moves only when every read succeeded, and only after the report has printed. A failed print restores the old marker.
- With no marker, the first run covers 7 days. `--since` is an ad-hoc look back that neither reads nor moves the marker. `--no-mark` gives a dry look, and agents must use it whenever they run the command for their own purposes.

**Sections, in order:**
1. **Waiting on you.**
   - Mentions of you in the window, and open PRs/MRs where you are reviewer or assignee.
   - Issues assigned to you and issues carrying the configured needs-a-human and decision labels. Only items created or updated in the window are listed in full; the standing backlog is one count line per list.
   - An issue on several lists is listed once and counted in each. `--all` lists everything.
2. **Merged since:** PRs/MRs merged in the window, grouped by the issue numbers in their titles or branches (ignore date-shaped branch segments). It also covers changelog entries added, where the repo has a configured changelog or records file.
3. **Decisions made:** comments in the window matching a configured ruling pattern, e.g. `Ruling (YYYY-MM-DD):`.
4. **Board movement:** issues opened and closed, counted by the configured priority tiers (labels first, milestone as fallback).
5. **Health:** the default branch's newest push pipeline/run and its failed jobs, a failed scheduled run on its own line, flaky jobs (passed only on retry more than once), and the configured release/registry tags.

**Output:** text by default, `--json` for the same data. Exit 0 only when every read succeeded. The slash command tells Claude to summarize with Waiting on you first, to state every FAILED part plainly, and to act on nothing unless asked.

**Config** (in forge-tracker's per-repo file): tier labels or milestone prefixes, the needs-human, decision and blocked label names, the ruling pattern, the changelog path, and the tags to report.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21), plus a small set of writes.

**`/groom`** keeps the tracker telling the truth, so that `/catchup` and `/next` rank real work. In practice the board drifts in predictable ways, and a ranking built on a drifted board ranks finished work as ready.

**The checks:**
- **Merged but still open:** an issue that a merged PR/MR references (`Closes #N`, `#N` in the title or branch) but that is still open. This is verified against the default branch, not taken on trust.
- **Labels disagreeing with milestones:** a tier label with no matching milestone, or a milestone whose tier label is missing.
- **A blocked label with nothing linked**, or links whose blocker is closed.
- **Decided but still waiting:** an issue labelled needs-a-human or decision that has a ruling comment after the label was added.
- **Stale branches:** remote branches with no open PR/MR whose commits are all on the default branch, so they are candidates to delete.
- **Stale or conflicted PRs/MRs:** open ones with merge conflicts, or no activity for N days.
- **Likely duplicates:** title and term similarity among open issues and those closed recently.
- **Placeholder due dates** shared by many issues, which skew any ordering by due date.

**Behaviour:**
- **Report first, read-only by default.** Every proposed change is listed with its evidence. Nothing is written until the user approves, item by item or as a batch.
- **Approved writes:** close with a resolution comment naming the PR/MR, fix labels or milestones, remove a blocked label, delete a merged branch. Each goes through forge-tracker's optional write-wrapper (#12), so a repo can enforce its own scrubbing or comment format.
- **Never acts on an inference it couldn't verify:** an "unclear" bucket is left for the user.
- **Output:** text and `--json`, with FAILED reads stated plainly, never as an empty section.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). A read-only forge layer that the briefing and grooming commands use. It is filed as its own piece, because the three commands built on it each need the same reads on all three forges.

**The forges.** GitHub (`gh`, REST plus GraphQL where REST is thin), GitLab (`glab api`, including self-hosted with a subpath and a pinned CA) and Forgejo/Gitea (`tea` where it covers the read, otherwise the REST API with the user's token). Each forge is detected from the repo's remote, the same way #12 already plans.

- **Identity:** the authenticated user, and whether an account is a bot.

Found while settling the last question on [lokkju/skills#13](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/13), on Claude Code 2.1.286 in headless `claude -p` runs with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, session-decisions 2026.10.15.1 installed.

**What happens.** The parent creates D1 with TaskCreate. A background subagent (`Agent` with `run_in_background: true`) is told the user answered D1 and to settle it. The subagent has no TaskUpdate: it isn't in its tool list and `ToolSearch` `select:TaskUpdate` answers "No matching deferred tools found". So it calls `decision_close`, which refuses:

> session-decisions: D1 is a task-list item; mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description. If TaskUpdate is deferred, load it with ToolSearch first.

The ruling is recorded nowhere and the task file stays pending. `decision_update` goes through the same `TaskUpdate` check, so I'd expect it to dead-end the same way (not run).

**Why.** `taskUpdateOffered()` in `hooks/register.tsx` asks `$.tool.list()`. A probe hook logged that list inside the subagent's `decision_close` call (the `tool.call` event carried the subagent's `agentId`), and it named TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskStop and TaskUpdate: the main loop's tools, not the subagent's. The declaration says "the tools the model can call now", which isn't what it returned for a subagent's loop.

**Related, documentation only.** A background subagent gets no TaskCreate either, so its items go through `decision_add` and are ledger items: they share the parent's queue and counter (the subagent's item came back as D2 after the parent's D1) but never appear in ctrl+t, even though the parent's do. The README's "Without them" paragraph and the ctrl+t limit describe a session with no task tools; they don't cover a session whose background subagents lack them. A foreground subagent does get TaskCreate, and its items land in the parent's task list with the parent's labels.

The fix is the maintainer's call; options I can see are deciding from the loop (`e.agentId` is set on a subagent's `tool.call`, and `$.agent.list()` lists the loop by that id, though it has no background flag), or letting `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the call comes from a subagent.

**`/next`** recommends what to work on: the user's own queue, work agents can start now, and what is blocked. It is read-only. It recommends, and never claims, assigns, comments or branches.

**Two layers, both cached outside the repo** under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/next/<host>_<project>/`:
1. **Facts (a script).**
   - **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state; branches with no PR/MR.
   - **How it caches:** under a fingerprint of cheap inputs. These are the default-branch head, the newest issue, PR and pipeline `updated_at`, open issue and PR counts, a digest of the milestones (id, title, due date), the remote branch heads, and a schema tag that hashes the code itself. When the fingerprint is unchanged, the cached facts are reused, so a rerun takes seconds. A run with a failed read is written but never reused.
2. **The slate (Claude's ranking).** It is stored with the facts' fingerprint and shown again unchanged until the fingerprint moves.
   - **The user's queue:** person-only items, ordered by how many agent-ready items each one unblocks, counted transitively through blocking links and cycle-safe.
   - **Agent lanes:** unblocked agent-ready items by tier and due date, grouped into lanes that shouldn't touch the same files. The grouping is a stated judgement, not a measurement. A lane that already has an open PR or a pushed branch is marked in flight.
   - **Blocked:** each blocked item and what it waits on.

**Classification rules learned the hard way:**
- **What person-only means:** the configured decision or needs-human labels, plus configurable keyword markers (e.g. hardware, legal).
- **Not person-only:** an assignee is never a reason, because agents share the user's account. Show the assignee as an owner. Some markers are only hints Claude may overrule; design work an agent can build is one example.
- **Merged-but-open issues inflate the ready list badly.** Flag issues that a merged PR/MR references but that are still open. That check, and fixing it, belongs to `/groom` (#22).

**Future enhancement, not now:** a status pane that shows the slate's top items, its age and a "stale" flag when the fingerprint moves. It reads only the cache, and shares a display mechanism with the session-decisions pane.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Each command can ship for one forge first, but the layer is what makes it work on GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo alike.

**`/catchup`** is for coming back to a project after time away: what changed, and what is waiting on you. It is read-only: no claims, comments or merges.

**The window:**
- It starts where the user's previous successful `/catchup` ended, kept in a local marker. **Not** at "your last forge activity": agents act under the user's account, and in practice that gives a four-minute window opening at an agent's last push.
- The marker lives under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/catchup/<host>_<project>_<user>.json`. The directory is 0700 and files 0600, writes are atomic, and a relative XDG value is ignored.
- The next window starts a few minutes before the marker, so a fast local clock can't skip events. Seeing an event twice is harmless.
- The marker moves only when every read succeeded, and only after the report has printed. A failed print restores the old marker.
- With no marker, the first run covers 7 days. `--since` is an ad-hoc look back that neither reads nor moves the marker. `--no-mark` gives a dry look, and agents must use it whenever they run the command for their own purposes.

**Sections, in order:**
1. **Waiting on you.**
   - Mentions of you in the window, and open PRs/MRs where you are reviewer or assignee.
   - Issues assigned to you and issues carrying the configured needs-a-human and decision labels. Only items created or updated in the window are listed in full; the standing backlog is one count line per list.
   - An issue on several lists is listed once and counted in each. `--all` lists everything.
2. **Merged since:** PRs/MRs merged in the window, grouped by the issue numbers in their titles or branches (ignore date-shaped branch segments). It also covers changelog entries added, where the repo has a configured changelog or records file.
3. **Decisions made:** comments in the window matching a configured ruling pattern, e.g. `Ruling (YYYY-MM-DD):`.
4. **Board movement:** issues opened and closed, counted by the configured priority tiers (labels first, milestone as fallback).
5. **Health:** the default branch's newest push pipeline/run and its failed jobs, a failed scheduled run on its own line, flaky jobs (passed only on retry more than once), and the configured release/registry tags.

**Output:** text by default, `--json` for the same data. Exit 0 only when every read succeeded. The slash command tells Claude to summarize with Waiting on you first, to state every FAILED part plainly, and to act on nothing unless asked.

**Config** (in forge-tracker's per-repo file): tier labels or milestone prefixes, the needs-human, decision and blocked label names, the ruling pattern, the changelog path, and the tags to report.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21), plus a small set of writes.

**`/groom`** keeps the tracker telling the truth, so that `/catchup` and `/next` rank real work. In practice the board drifts in predictable ways, and a ranking built on a drifted board ranks finished work as ready.

**The checks:**
- **Merged but still open:** an issue that a merged PR/MR references (`Closes #N`, `#N` in the title or branch) but that is still open. This is verified against the default branch, not taken on trust.
- **Labels disagreeing with milestones:** a tier label with no matching milestone, or a milestone whose tier label is missing.
- **A blocked label with nothing linked**, or links whose blocker is closed.
- **Decided but still waiting:** an issue labelled needs-a-human or decision that has a ruling comment after the label was added.
- **Stale branches:** remote branches with no open PR/MR whose commits are all on the default branch, so they are candidates to delete.
- **Stale or conflicted PRs/MRs:** open ones with merge conflicts, or no activity for N days.
- **Likely duplicates:** title and term similarity among open issues and those closed recently.
- **Placeholder due dates** shared by many issues, which skew any ordering by due date.

**Behaviour:**
- **Report first, read-only by default.** Every proposed change is listed with its evidence. Nothing is written until the user approves, item by item or as a batch.
- **Approved writes:** close with a resolution comment naming the PR/MR, fix labels or milestones, remove a blocked label, delete a merged branch. Each goes through forge-tracker's optional write-wrapper (#12), so a repo can enforce its own scrubbing or comment format.
- **Never acts on an inference it couldn't verify:** an "unclear" bucket is left for the user.
- **Output:** text and `--json`, with FAILED reads stated plainly, never as an empty section.

_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#6._

The forge-release skill's decision tree currently routes CalVer (and anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps) to yeet, SemVer packages on GitHub to release-please, and Rust crates to release-plz. The question is whether the middle branch should go to yeet too, so one tool covers every non-crate repo. The python-project skill's release-please default would follow whatever this decides.

## The case for keeping release-please, checked

- **Native version files.** Weaker than it sounds. Neither tool updates `uv.lock`: release-please has googleapis/release-please#2561 open for it. yeet updates `pyproject.toml` through a marker comment (`version = "1.2.3" # x-yeet-version`) and `package.json` through `json_pointer: /version`, which covers the files these repos publish from.
- **Tokens.** No difference. Both run on `GITHUB_TOKEN` when the publish step lives in the release workflow, and both need a GitHub App token only when the release has to start another workflow (one of my sites' deploy does).
- **Maturity.** The real one. yeet (monkescience/yeet, MIT) was created in February 2026 and has 4 contributors and 7 stars; release-please is Google's and widely used.
- **Language plugins.** release-please has strategies and plugins for Java, Ruby, PHP, Helm and node or cargo workspaces. None of these repos use them.

## Why the maturity risk is small here

- yeet runs as a container pinned by digest, so an abandoned yeet keeps working at the pinned version.
- Its only state is git tags and `CHANGELOG.md`, both tool-agnostic, so leaving it is a config swap. yeet's docs carry a migrate-from-release-please guide, and the reverse is the same shape.
- Telemetry is on by default; the skill already sets `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

## What standardizing gets

One tool, one `.yeet.yaml` shape and one App pattern across GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps, for CalVer and SemVer. The skill's decision tree drops a branch, and its references drop the release-please setup and troubleshooting.

## Proposal

- New repos: yeet, SemVer or CalVer.
- Rust crates: release-plz stays. It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't.
- Repos on release-please today move only when someone is in them anyway: lokkju/dbxdebug, lokkju/git-spreader and two private repos. release-plz today: lokkju/neovision and two private repos.
- python-project switches its release default to yeet.

## Not yet checked

- How yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the project's own version (a release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml` but not `uv.lock` would fail `uv sync --locked`). release-please has the same gap; the usual fixes are a dynamic version (hatch-vcs) or a follow-up `uv lock` commit on the release branch.
- yeet's monorepo targets against release-please's linked versions, if a multi-package repo ever needs them.

The skill says that every question or step only the user can do goes in the queue in the same turn. Nothing enforces it. An assistant can end a reply with a "left for you" list (merge these PRs, run this on each host) and queue none of it. Wording alone relies on the model applying the rule at the moment it writes the closing list, and that is where it slips. The usual rationalization is that a step the assistant could do on request (merging a PR) isn't "only the user's".

## Proposal

- **A `classic.Stop` handler in `hooks/register.tsx`.** It reads `last_assistant_message` and skips when `stop_hook_active` is set. It finds hand-off lines that carry no `D<n>`/`A<n>` label: phrases such as "left for you", "you'll need to", "your call" and "next steps", plus the bullets or numbered items that follow them. When it finds any, it returns `block` with a reason that quotes those lines and says to queue them and rewrite the reply. The reason also says to ignore a match that isn't a hand-off.
- **The detector in `hooks/queue.ts` or `hooks/subject.ts`,** as plain data, with tests for:
  - hand-offs with labels
  - hand-offs without labels
  - prose that only resembles one
- **One line in SKILL.md:** anything handed back to the user counts, including merges and per-host steps the assistant could do if asked.
- **Release:** a minor version, 2.1.0.

## Costs and open questions

- It adds one model pass to each reply where it fires.
- Phrase matching misfires both ways. The phrase list and the threshold need tuning against real transcripts before it blocks by default. One option is to start it as an `additionalContext` nudge rather than a block.
- It's unclear whether the fallback-ledger mode (no TaskCreate) needs the same check, since its replies already end with a list of open items.

Follow-up from #18, which fixes #9.

## What isn't proven

In #9, ledger items A38 to A40 vanished when the task tools came back. #18 fixes the merge in `hydrate()`, so items in plugin state and the stored record survive a re-read of the task files. Why the stored record lacked those items in the first place is unproven.

The likeliest cause: the session resumed under a **new session id** while `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` kept the old task list. The plugin keys its stored record by session id (`session:<sid>` in `$.store`), so the resumed session read an empty record. #18's second register test simulates that, but nobody has confirmed it against a real resume.

## What to do

1. Confirm what happens to the session id and the plugin store across a resume, a `/exit` and restart of a background job, and a compaction. If the id changes, find whether `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` or the tasks directory stays stable.
2. If the id changes while the task list stays, key the stored record (counters, the `created` map, the ledger, the `closed` rulings) by the task list id when one is set, and fall back to the session id otherwise. Migrate an existing `session:<sid>` record the first time.
3. Add tests for a resume with a new session id and the same task list, plus the migration.
4. Update the README's "How it stays in sync" and "Limits" sections.

## Where to start

`plugins/session-decisions/hooks/register.tsx`: `loadRecord`, `persist`, `prune` and `hydrate`. If #18 isn't merged when you start, branch from `fix/sd-tools-gap` and say in the PR that it's stacked on #18.

items.body:
Follow-up from #18, which fixes #9.

## What #18 assumes

`decision_close` now settles a task-list item only when TaskUpdate isn't in the session's tool list. It checks that with `$.tool.list()`, which the engine's declarations describe as "the tools the model can call now". Nobody has checked whether that list includes a **deferred** tool the model hasn't loaded through ToolSearch yet. TaskCreate, TaskList, TaskUpdate and TaskGet are deferred in the sessions that have them.

If `$.tool.list()` leaves deferred tools out, `decision_close` accepts a task-list item even though TaskUpdate exists. The item shows as settled in the queue, but its task file stays open, so ctrl+t and the task list disagree with the queue.

## What to do

1. Find out what `$.tool.list()` returns for a deferred tool. Check the engine's type declarations (run `/plugin-types` in Claude Code to write them for the current build) and the test harness. If neither settles it, check a real session: load the plugin with `--plugin-dir` in a background or `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` session, where the task tools exist but are deferred, and log what `$.tool.list()` returns.
2. If deferred tools are missing, make the check see them. Use whatever the engine offers for deferred or known tools. Failing that, treat TaskUpdate as available whenever TaskCreate is known to have run in the session.
3. Add a test for the deferred case in `tests/register.test.tsx`.

## Where to start

`plugins/session-decisions/hooks/register.tsx`, the `decision_close` handler. #18 adds the `$.tool.list()` call. If #18 isn't merged when you start, branch from `fix/sd-tools-gap` and say in the PR that it's stacked on #18.

Stacked on [lokkju/skills#17](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/17): this branch starts from it, so its first commit shows here until #17 merges. Review the last two commits.

Design: [comment on #9](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/9#issuecomment-6136779661).

- `decision_close` settles a task-list item when `$.tool.list()` has no TaskUpdate (or the host can't list tools). The item is marked completed with the usual `Ruling (<date>): ...` line in plugin state, and a copy goes into a new `closed` map in the session's store record, keyed by task id. While TaskUpdate is offered, task items are still refused with a pointer to it, so the task file gets updated when it can be. The "not found" deny now fires only for a label that is nowhere in the queue: `session-decisions: D9 isn't in this session's decision queue.`
- `hydrate()` merges through a pure `mergeHydrated()` instead of replacing: ledger items are the stored ledger plus those already in state (state wins), a stored ruling overrides a task file that still shows its item open, and a settled item whose task file has gone stays settled.
- A later TaskUpdate that sets the task's status drops the stored ruling, since the task file has the status then.
- Ledger items made while the task tools were missing stay ledger items and stay closable with `decision_close`.
- README ("How it stays in sync", "Limits") and SKILL.md describe what happens when the tools come and go, including that ctrl+t still shows an item settled this way as pending.

Tests: `mergeHydrated()` and `settle()` in `tests/queue.test.ts`. In `tests/register.test.tsx`, closing a task item is refused while TaskUpdate is offered, then settles it once the tool list is empty, the task file stays pending, the resume reminder leaves it out and `/decisions all` shows it completed with its ruling, and unknown labels are still refused. A second test resumes under a new session id with the same `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID`, so the store record comes back empty, and checks that the ledger item and the stored ruling survive, and that the ledger item closes with `decision_close` after the tools return. 28 pass; `tsc` and `claude plugin validate --strict` are clean.

The cause of the vanished ledger in #9 isn't proven. `hydrate()` already read the stored ledger, so the record it read must have lacked A38 to A40; a resume that changed the session id while the task list id held fits that, and is what the second test simulates. The merge covers it when plugin state survives the resume. If state doesn't survive either, keying the store record by the task list id would be the next step; this PR doesn't do that.

Fixes #9
